steps.title: Pass an approved role to EC2

blocks.text: Profile attachment and application permission evidence are separate checks.
An instance profile holds one IAM role and is the mechanism for passing that role to EC2.
Attach the approved profile with associate-iam-instance-profile when no association exists. Replace an existing profile through the console’s Modify IAM role workflow.
Use the instance role credential provider, not embedded keys. Inspect caller identity and test one allowed and one denied operation under the assigned role’s permissions.

steps.title: Work through the evidence: Pass an approved role to EC2

blocks.text: Review whether this is a new association or a profile replacement, selecting the supplied association operation or Modify IAM role workflow accordingly. From the instance, inspect caller identity under the role credential provider and retain the supplied allowed/denied operation outcomes with the assigned role context.
An attached profile does not prove the application’s intended access. It passes one role, not embedded access keys.

steps.title: A closer look: Pass an approved role to EC2

segments.label: Attach an existing IAM role and confirm a successful request
segments.summary: An existing role, DemoRoleForEC2, has an IAM read-only policy. The console workflow opens the instance’s Actions menu, selects Security and Modify IAM role, chooses that role, and saves the change. The instance’s Security information then identifies the attached role. Running aws iam list-users from the instance returns user information without running aws configure. This demonstrates attachment and a successful request, but does not establish the profile–role distinction or complete the caller-identity and allowed/denied verification.

blocks.group_title: Attach the approved role through the EC2 IAM-role setting

bridge.before: Watch the Modify IAM role workflow and the successful request afterward. The clip uses the console’s role terminology; Devspace distinguishes the role from the instance profile that passes it to EC2.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates console attachment and one successful request. The text also explains the one-role profile, command-based attachment, role credential provider, caller-identity inspection, and both permission tests without changing the approved permissions.

steps.title: Check pass an approved role to EC2
steps.lede: Read the supplied evidence in this step and choose the interpretation it supports.

public.prompt: What verifies role identity and bounded permissions from the EC2 instance?

options.text: Use its role credential provider without embedded keys; check caller identity, then record a supplied allowed success and denied rejection under that role.
Use embedded keys and record only a successful operation.
Check only that an IAM-role setting exists.

o1.message: This follows the stated evidence and the taught verification rule.

o2.message: Embedded keys do not verify the instance’s assigned role provider; one success also omits the denial check.

o3.message: The setting alone omits caller identity and allowed/denied access outcomes.

correct.message: Your choice follows the stated evidence and verification rule.

incorrect.message: Recheck the evidence and the explanation for the selected option.

hints: Tie identity and both access outcomes to the same credential context.

buckets.label: Meets the stated criterion / conclusion supported

items.text: Instance IAM-role setting: approved instance profile containing one approved role. Role credential provider used; no embedded keys. Caller identity matches assigned role. Supplied allowed operation succeeds; supplied denied operation rejected. Both outcomes recorded beside assigned role context.

Approved profile containing one role is assigned, but script uses embedded keys for a different identity. Allowed operation succeeds; denied operation rejected.
Conclusion: assigned instance role’s permissions verified.

Approved profile and role provider; caller identity matches. Both supplied allowed and supplied denied operations succeed.
Conclusion: bounded assigned-role access verified.

i1.message: Approved profile, one role, caller identity and both permission outcomes are verified without embedded keys.

i2.message: The operations use a different credential identity, so they do not verify the assigned role provider or its permissions.

i3.message: The supplied denied operation must be rejected to demonstrate the required boundary.

correct.message: Each judgement follows the supplied excerpt and the verification criterion.

incorrect.message: Check the evidence behind each conclusion; a partial success does not establish every required boundary.

hints: A success matters only when identity and credential context match the assigned role.

steps.title: Scope EKS Pod Identity to the workload

blocks.text: The association belongs to a specific workload identity context.
EKS Pod Identity links an IAM role for application AWS access to a Kubernetes service account within a namespace and cluster.
Create the association with the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and approved role. The workload must use that serviceAccountName.
The Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain deliver temporary role credentials to associated Pods. Verify intended-workload allowed access and unassociated-workload rejection.

Review the association’s cluster, namespace, service account and role beside the workload’s serviceAccountName. Keep the Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential-chain qualification in the credential explanation. Compare intended-workload allowed access with the supplied unassociated-workload rejection; one Pod’s access is not another’s evidence.
A role’s existence is not the association. The serviceAccountName must match the scoped association, with the stated agent and SDK support.

blocks.text: Temporary credentials still require an approved token-context trust boundary.
GitHub Actions OIDC lets a workflow obtain temporary AWS role credentials without storing AWS access keys.
Configure the GitHub token issuer as an IAM OIDC provider. Restrict role-trust aud and sub to the approved audience and repository/branch or environment.
Grant workflow id-token: write and configure the AWS credential action for the approved role. Test that an unapproved repository or branch cannot assume it.

left.title: Trust context
left.alt_text: Trust context: GitHub token issuer; IAM OIDC provider; aud: approved audience; sub: approved repository/branch or environment

right.title: Workflow review
right.alt_text: Workflow review: Workflow id-token: write; AWS credential action: approved role; Approved token context: expect success; Unapproved repository/branch: expect rejection

blocks.takeaway: Review the issuer and both aud/sub restrictions alongside the credential action’s approved role. Token permission alone does not establish role trust.

steps.title: Work through the evidence: Review workflow federation trust

blocks.text: Compare the supplied issuer, aud and sub restrictions with the approved context. Review id-token: write and the AWS credential action’s role target. Keep the approved success and supplied unapproved repository/branch rejection together. Check the audience separately; a matching subject alone is not every trust test.
No stored keys does not mean unrestricted trust is acceptable. Workflow token permission alone does not establish the AWS role’s intended trust boundary.

steps.title: A closer look: Review workflow federation trust

segments.label: Request a GitHub token and verify AWS authentication
segments.summary: The workflow requests permission to generate a GitHub OIDC token, then uses the AWS credentials action to exchange that token for temporary credentials for an AWS role. It lists S3 buckets as a positive authentication check. After pushing the workflow, the presenter opens its Actions run and inspects the successful bucket-listing result. This demonstrates authentication without long-lived AWS access keys, but does not establish that unapproved workflows are rejected.

blocks.group_title: GitHub OIDC authentication from workflow to AWS

bridge.before: Watch how token permission and the AWS credentials action lead to a successful authentication check. The AWS role and provider are already configured for this demonstration.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates keyless authentication, not the complete trust boundary. The text covers IAM provider setup, aud/sub restrictions, explicit id-token: write permission, and rejection testing for an unapproved repository or branch.

steps.title: Check review workflow federation trust
steps.lede: Read the supplied evidence in this step and choose the interpretation it supports.

public.prompt: Which GitHub OIDC setup and test verifies approved-workflow access while excluding an unapproved repository or branch?

options.text: Grant id-token: write, leave aud and sub unrestricted, and test only the approved workflow.
Restrict aud but allow any repository/branch and treat an unapproved success as acceptable.
Constrain aud and sub to the approved context, grant id-token: write, configure the credential action for the approved role, and verify approved success plus unapproved rejection.

o1.message: Token permission alone does not constrain role trust or demonstrate rejection of the unapproved case.

o2.message: The supplied repository/branch restriction and negative access test are required, not just the audience condition.

o3.message: This follows the stated evidence and the taught verification rule.

incorrect.message: Recheck the evidence and the explanation for the selected option.

items.text: GitHub token issuer configured as IAM OIDC provider. Role trust accepts only supplied approved aud and sub repository/branch. Workflow id-token: write; AWS credential action assumes approved role without stored AWS keys. Approved workflow gets temporary intended-role credentials; supplied unapproved repository/branch is rejected; separate wrong-audience case is rejected.

GitHub IAM OIDC provider and restricted sub; aud accepts any audience. Workflow has id-token: write and approved-role credential action; no stored keys. Approved workflow succeeds and unapproved branch rejected, but wrong audience also succeeds.
Conclusion: approved audience boundary separately verified.

GitHub OIDC provider and restricted aud; sub accepts any repository/branch. Approved workflow gets temporary role credentials without stored keys; supplied unapproved repository also succeeds.
Conclusion: approved repository/branch boundary verified.

i1.message: Provider, both claim restrictions, workflow permission/action and all contrasting access cases verify the stated boundary.

i2.message: Rejecting the unapproved branch does not compensate for accepting an unapproved audience.

i3.message: The required unapproved repository/branch case must be rejected.

incorrect.message: Check the evidence behind each conclusion; a partial success does not establish every required boundary.

blocks.text: Keep credential composition, lifetime and grant distinctions visible.
Temporary AWS credentials have three parts: access key ID, secret access key and session token. They expire after their issued lifetime.
Use aws sts assume-role with --role-arn, --role-session-name and the approved --duration-seconds. Use all three returned credential fields and inspect Expiration.

Role identity-based grants intersect with any session policies. Resource-based grants are evaluated separately; grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies. An applicable explicit deny overrides an allow.

steps.title: Work through the evidence: Inspect a bounded STS session

blocks.text: Review the approved role, session name and duration beside Expiration and the three credential-field names, without displaying values. Apply session-policy intersection to role identity-based grants, not every resource-based grant. Direct session-ARN grants are not limited by session policies; an applicable explicit deny still overrides allow.
An access-key pair alone omits the session token. Session-policy intersection is not an unqualified limit on every resource-based grant.

steps.title: Check inspect a bounded STS session
steps.lede: Read the supplied evidence in this step and choose the interpretation it supports.

public.prompt: For a supplied operation, the role identity policy allows it but an applicable session policy does not; no resource-based grant exists and no other policy contributes an allow. What follows?

options.text: The identity-policy grant is limited by the intersection with the session policy, so this evidence does not permit the operation.
The role allow alone overrides the session policy.
A direct-session-ARN exception automatically applies even with no resource-based grant.

o1.message: This follows the stated evidence and the taught verification rule.

o2.message: Role identity-policy grants are intersected with any session policy.

o3.message: That exception concerns grants directly to the session ARN; this case explicitly has no resource-based grant.

correct.message: Your choice follows the stated evidence and verification rule.

incorrect.message: Recheck the evidence and the explanation for the selected option.

hints: Identify the source of the allow before applying the session-policy rule.

steps.lede: Read the supplied excerpts in this step and decide which are correct, defective or unsafe.

public.prompt: Read each bounded STS request/credential or permission-evidence record. Decide whether its stated conclusion is supported. No credential values are shown.

buckets.label: Meets the stated criterion / conclusion supported
Does not meet the criterion / conclusion unsupported

items.text:
aws sts assume-role uses supplied approved --role-arn, --role-session-name and --duration-seconds. Returned access key ID, secret access key and session token all used with values concealed. Expiration and issued lifetime recorded and match approved duration.
Conclusion: bounded complete session configuration verified.

Request matches approved role, session name and duration. Only access key ID and secret access key used; session token omitted. Expiration is not inspected.
Conclusion: complete temporary credentials and approved lifetime verified.

Permission evidence: only role identity-based grant allows supplied operation; session policy does not allow it. No resource-based grant or other allow; no explicit deny.
Conclusion: this operation is not permitted by the role/session intersection.

Permission evidence: resource-based permission directly grants the supplied operation to the session ARN. Session policy does not allow it; no applicable explicit deny and no other limitations in supplied evidence.
Conclusion: this direct-session-ARN grant is not limited by that session policy.

Permission evidence: resource-based grant directly to session ARN allows operation; an applicable policy explicitly denies that same operation.
Conclusion: the direct-session-ARN exception means the operation is allowed despite the deny.

i1.message: The approved request, all three concealed credential fields and approved expiry/lifetime are present.

i2.message: Temporary credentials also require the session token; approved expiry must be inspected rather than assumed.

i3.message: A role identity-based allow is limited by the session-policy intersection in this supplied case.

i4.message: The direct-session-ARN exception must be preserved for this separately evaluated resource-based grant.

i5.message: An applicable explicit deny overrides the allow, including a direct-session-ARN grant.

correct.message: Each judgement follows the supplied excerpt and the verification criterion.

incorrect.message: Check the evidence behind each conclusion; a partial success does not establish every required boundary.

hints: First identify the grant source; distinguish a direct session-ARN grant from role identity grants and apply any explicit deny.

blocks.text: Pass one approved role through the profile; inspect caller identity and role-provider allowed/denied operation evidence.

Constrain issuer, aud and sub; retain approved success and unapproved-context rejection evidence.
Use all three temporary credential fields and inspect expiry; preserve the role/session/resource grant distinctions and explicit-deny override.
